# Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims] Contents

## 1. Introduction

## 1.1

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 1.1] 1.1.1  This Protocol is primarily designed for personal injury claims which are likely to be allocated to the fast track and to the entirety of those claims: not only to the personal injury element of a claim which also includes, for instance, property damage. It is not intended to apply to claims which proceed under—

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 1.1] (a) the Pre-Action Protocol for Low Value Personal Injury Claims in Road Traffic Accidents from 31 July 2013;

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 1.1] (b) the Pre-Action Protocol for Low Value Personal Injury (Employers’ Liability and Public Liability) Claims;

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 1.1] (c) the Pre-Action Protocol for the Resolution of Clinical Disputes;

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 1.1] (d) the Pre-Action Protocol for Disease and Illness Claims; or

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 1.1] (e) the Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims below the small claims limit in road traffic accidents (“the RTA Small Claims Protocol”)

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 1.1] 1.1.2  If at any stage the claimant values the claim at more than the upper limit of the fast track, the claimant should notify the defendant as soon as possible. However, the “cards on the table” approach advocated by this Protocol is equally appropriate to higher value claims. The spirit, if not the letter of the Protocol, should still be followed for claims which could potentially be allocated to the intermediate track or multi-track. All parties are expected to consider the Serious Injury Guide in any claim to which that Guide applies ( http://www.seriousinjuryguide.co.uk/ (opens in a new tab) ).

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 1.1] 1.2 Claims which exit either of the low value pre-action protocols listed at paragraph 1.1.1(a) and (b) (“the low value protocols”) prior to Stage 2, or the RTA Small Claims Protocol, will proceed under this Protocol from the point specified in those protocols, and as set out in paragraph 1.3.

## 1.3

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 1.3] 1.3.1  Where a claim exits a low value protocol because the defendant considers that there is inadequate mandatory information in the Claim Notification Form (“CNF”), the claim will proceed under this Protocol from paragraph 5.1.

## 1.3.2  Where in a claim under either low value protocol a defendant—

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 1.3.2  Where in a claim under either low value protocol a defendant—] (a) alleges contributory negligence;

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 1.3.2  Where in a claim under either low value protocol a defendant—] (b) does not complete and send the CNF Response; or

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 1.3.2  Where in a claim under either low value protocol a defendant—] (c) does not admit liability,

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 1.3.2  Where in a claim under either low value protocol a defendant—] the claim will proceed under this Protocol from paragraph 5.5.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 1.3.2  Where in a claim under either low value protocol a defendant—] 1.3.3 Where a claim exits the RTA Small Claims Protocol and is directed to this Protocol, the claim will proceed under this Protocol from paragraph 5.5.

## 1.4

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 1.4] 1.4.1  This Protocol sets out conduct that the court would normally expect prospective parties to follow prior to the commencement of proceedings. It establishes a reasonable process and timetable for the exchange of information relevant to a dispute, sets standards for the content and quality of letters of claim, and in particular, the conduct of pre-action negotiations. In particular, the parts of this Protocol that are concerned with rehabilitation are likely to be of application in all claims.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 1.4] 1.4.2  The timetable and the arrangements for disclosing documents and obtaining expert evidence may need to be varied to suit the circumstances of the case. Where one or both parties consider the detail of the Protocol is not appropriate to the case, and proceedings are subsequently issued, the court will expect an explanation as to why the Protocol has not been followed, or has been varied.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 1.4] 1.5 Where either party fails to comply with this Protocol, the court may impose sanctions. When deciding whether to do so, the court will look at whether the parties have complied in substance with the relevant principles and requirements. It will also consider the effect any non-compliance has had on another party. It is not likely to be concerned with minor or technical shortcomings (see paragraphs 13 to 15 of the Practice Direction on Pre-Action Conduct and Protocols).

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 1.4] To the top

## Early Issue

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > Early Issue] 1.6 The Protocol recommends that a defendant be given three months to investigate and respond to a claim before proceedings are issued. This may not always be possible, particularly where a claimant only consults a legal representative close to the end of any relevant limitation period. In these circumstances, the claimant’s solicitor should give as much notice of the intention to issue proceedings as is practicable and the parties should consider whether the court might be invited to extend time for service of the claimant’s supporting documents and for service of any defence, or alternatively, to stay the proceedings while the recommended steps in the Protocol are followed.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > Early Issue] To the top

## Litigants in Person

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > Litigants in Person] 1.7 If a party to the claim does not have a legal representative they should still, in so far as reasonably possible, fully comply with this Protocol. Any reference to a claimant in this Protocol will also mean the claimant’s legal representative.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > Litigants in Person] To the top

## 2. Overview of Protocol – General Aim

## 2.1 The Protocol’s objectives are to—

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 2.1 The Protocol’s objectives are to—] (a) encourage the exchange of early and full information about the dispute;

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 2.1 The Protocol’s objectives are to—] (b) encourage better and earlier pre-action investigation by all parties;

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 2.1 The Protocol’s objectives are to—] (c) enable the parties to avoid litigation by agreeing a settlement of the dispute before proceedings are commenced;

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 2.1 The Protocol’s objectives are to—] (d) support the just, proportionate and efficient management of proceedings where litigation cannot be avoided; and

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 2.1 The Protocol’s objectives are to—] (e) promote the provision of medical or rehabilitation treatment (not just in high value cases) to address the needs of the Claimant at the earliest possible opportunity.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 2.1 The Protocol’s objectives are to—] To the top

## 3. The Protocol

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 3. The Protocol] An illustrative flow chart is attached at Annexe A which shows each of the steps that the parties are expected to take before the commencement of proceedings.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 3. The Protocol] To the top

## Letter of Notification

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > Letter of Notification] 3.1 The claimant or his legal representative may wish to notify a defendant and/or the insurer as soon as they know a claim is likely to be made, but before they are able to send a detailed Letter of Claim, particularly, for instance, when the defendant has no or limited knowledge of the incident giving rise to the claim, or where the claimant is incurring significant expenditure as a result of the accident which he hopes the defendant might pay for, in whole or in part.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > Letter of Notification] 3.2 The Letter of Notification should advise the defendant and/or the insurer of any relevant information that is available to assist with determining issues of liability/suitability of the claim for an interim payment and/or early rehabilitation.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > Letter of Notification] 3.3 If the claimant or his legal representative gives notification before sending a Letter of Claim, it will not start the timetable for the Letter of Response. However the Letter of Notification should be acknowledged within 14 days of receipt.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > Letter of Notification] To the top

## 4. Rehabilitation

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 4. Rehabilitation] 4.1 The parties should consider as early as possible whether the claimant has reasonable needs that could be met by medical treatment or other rehabilitative measures. They should discuss how these needs might be addressed.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 4. Rehabilitation] 4.2 The Rehabilitation Code (which can be found at: http://www.iua.co.uk/IUA_Member/Publications (opens in a new tab) ) is likely to be helpful in considering how to identify the claimant’s needs and how to address the cost of providing for those needs.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 4. Rehabilitation] 4.3 The time limit set out in paragraph 6.3 of this Protocol shall not be shortened, except by consent to allow these issues to be addressed.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 4. Rehabilitation] 4.4 Any immediate needs assessment report or documents associated with it that are obtained for the purposes of rehabilitation shall not be used in the litigation except by consent and shall in any event be exempt from the provisions of paragraphs 7.2 to 7.11 of this Protocol. Similarly, persons conducting the immediate needs assessment shall not be a compellable witness at court.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 4. Rehabilitation] 4.5 Consideration of rehabilitation options, by all parties, should be an on going process throughout the entire Protocol period.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 4. Rehabilitation] To the top

## 5. Letter of Claim

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 5. Letter of Claim] 5.1 Subject to paragraph 5.3 the claimant should send to the proposed defendant two copies of the Letter of Claim. One copy of the letter is for the defendant, the second for passing on to the insurers, as soon as possible, and, in any event, within 7 days of the day upon which the defendant received it.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 5. Letter of Claim] 5.2 The Letter of Claim should include the information described on the template at Annexe B1. The level of detail will need to be varied to suit the particular circumstances. In all cases there should be sufficient information for the defendant to assess liability and to enable the defendant to estimate the likely size and heads of the claim without necessarily addressing quantum in detail.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 5. Letter of Claim] 5.3 The letter should contain a clear summary of the facts on which the claim is based together with an indication of the nature of any injuries suffered, and the way in which these impact on the claimant’s day to day functioning and prognosis. Any financial loss incurred by the claimant should be outlined with an indication of the heads of damage to be claimed and the amount of that loss, unless this is impracticable.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 5. Letter of Claim] 5.4 Details of the claimant’s National Insurance number and date of birth should be supplied to the defendant’s insurer once the defendant has responded to the Letter of Claim and confirmed the identity of the insurer. This information should not be supplied in the Letter of Claim.

## 5.5

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 5.5] 5.5.1 Where a claim no longer continues under either low value protocol, the CNF completed by the claimant under those protocols can be used as the Letter of Claim under this Protocol unless the defendant has notified the claimant that there is inadequate information in the CNF.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 5.5] 5.5.2 Where a claim no longer continues under the RTA Small Claims Protocol, the Small Claim Notification Form or SCNF completed by the claimant can be used as the Letter of Claim under this Protocol.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 5.5] 5.6 Once the claimant has sent the Letter of Claim no further investigation on liability should normally be carried out within the Protocol period until a response is received from the defendant indicating whether liability is disputed.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 5.5] To the top

## Status of Letters of Claim and Response

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > Status of Letters of Claim and Response] 5.7 Letters of Claim and Response are not intended to have the same formal status as a statement of case in proceedings. It would not be consistent with the spirit of the Protocol for a party to ‘take a point’ on this in the proceedings, provided that there was no obvious intention by the party who changed their position to mislead the other party.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > Status of Letters of Claim and Response] To the top

## 6. The Response

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 6. The Response] 6.1 Attached at Annexe B2 is a template for the suggested contents of the Letter of Response: the level of detail will need to be varied to suit the particular circumstances.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 6. The Response] 6.2 The defendant must reply within 21 calendar days of the date of posting of the letter identifying the insurer (if any). If the insurer is aware of any significant omissions from the letter of claim they should identify them specifically. Similarly, if they are aware that another defendant has also been identified whom they believe would not be a correct defendant in any proceedings, they should notify the claimant without delay, with reasons, and in any event by the end of the Response period. Where there has been no reply by the defendant or insurer within 21 days, the claimant will be entitled to issue proceedings. Compliance with this paragraph will be taken into account on the question of any assessment of the defendant’s costs.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 6. The Response] 6.3 The defendant (insurer) will have a maximum of three months from the date of acknowledgment of the Letter of Claim (or of the CNF or SCNF where the claim commenced in a portal) to investigate. No later than the end of that period, The defendant (insurer) should reply by no later than the end of that period, stating if liability is admitted by admitting that the accident occurred, that the accident was caused by the defendant’s breach of duty, and the claimant suffered loss and there is no defence under the Limitation Act 1980.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 6. The Response] 6.4 Where the accident occurred outside England and Wales and/or where the defendant is outside the jurisdiction, the time periods of 21 days and three months should normally be extended up to 42 days and six months.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 6. The Response] 6.5 If a  defendant denies liability and/or causation, their version of events should be supplied. The defendant should also enclose with the response, documents in their possession which are material to the issues between the parties, and which would be likely to be ordered to be disclosed by the court, either on an application for pre-action disclosure, or on disclosure during proceedings. No charge will be made for providing copy documents under the Protocol.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 6. The Response] 6.6 An admission made by any party under this Protocol may well be binding on that party in the litigation. Further information about admissions made under this Protocol is to be found in Civil Procedure Rules (“CPR”) rule 14.1A.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 6. The Response] 6.7 Following receipt of the Letter of Response, if the claimant is aware that there may be a delay of six months or more before the claimant decides if, when and how to proceed, the claimant should keep the defendant generally informed.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 6. The Response] To the top

## 7. Disclosure

## 7.1 Documents

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 7.1 Documents] 7.1.1  The aim of early disclosure of documents by the defendant is not to encourage ‘fishing expeditions’ by the claimant, but to promote an early exchange of relevant information to help in clarifying or resolving issues in dispute. The claimant’s solicitor can assist by identifying in the Letter of Claim or in a subsequent letter the particular categories of documents which they consider are relevant and why, with a brief explanation of their purported relevance if necessary.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 7.1 Documents] 7.1.2  Attached at Annexe C are specimen, but non-exhaustive, lists of documents likely to be material in different types of claim.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 7.1 Documents] 7.1.3  Pre-action disclosure will generally be limited to the documents required to be enclosed with the Letter of Claim and the Response. In cases where liability is admitted in full, disclosure will be limited to the documents relevant to quantum, the parties can agree that further disclosure may be given. If either or both of the parties consider that further disclosure should be given but there is disagreement about some aspect of that process, they may be able to make an application to the court for pre-action disclosure under Part 31 of the CPR. Parties should assist each other and avoid the necessity for such an application.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 7.1 Documents] 7.1.4  The protocol should also contain a requirement that the defendant is under a duty to preserve the disclosure documents and other evidence (CCTV for example). If the documents are destroyed, this could be an abuse of the court process.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 7.1 Documents] To the top

## Experts

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > Experts] A. Claims which do not consist of, or include, a claim for a whiplash injury

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > Experts] (whiplash injury is defined in paragraph 7.12.7)

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > Experts] 7.2 Save for cases likely to be allocated to the multi-track, the Protocol encourages joint selection of, and access to, quantum experts, and, on occasion liability experts e.g. engineers. The expert report produced is not a joint report for the purposes of CPR Part 35. The Protocol promotes the practice of the claimant obtaining a medical report, disclosing it to the defendant who then asks questions and/or agrees it and does not obtain their own report. The Protocol provides for nomination of the expert by the claimant in personal injury claims.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > Experts] 7.3 Before any party instructs an expert, they should give the other party a list of the name(s) of one or more experts in the relevant speciality whom they consider are suitable to instruct.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > Experts] 7.4 Some solicitors choose to obtain medical reports through medical agencies, rather than directly from a specific doctor or hospital. The defendant’s prior consent to this should be sought and, if the defendant so requests, the agency should be asked to provide in advance the names of the doctor(s) whom they are considering instructing.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > Experts] 7.5 Where a medical expert is to be instructed, the claimant’s solicitor will organise access to relevant medical records – see specimen letter of instruction at Annexe D.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > Experts] 7.6 Within 14 days of providing a list of experts the other party may indicate an objection to one or more of the named experts. The first party should then instruct a mutually acceptable expert assuming there is one (this is not the same as a joint expert). It must be emphasised that when the claimant nominates an expert in the original Letter of Claim, the defendant has a further 14 days to object to one or more of the named experts after expiration of the 21 day period within which they have to reply to the Letter of Claim, as set out in paragraph 6.2.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > Experts] 7.7 If the defendant objects to all the listed experts, the parties may then instruct experts of their own choice. It will be for the court to decide, subsequently and if proceedings are issued, whether either party had acted unreasonably.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > Experts] 7.8 If the defendant does not object to an expert nominated by the claimant, they shall not be entitled to rely on their own expert evidence within that expert’s area of expertise unless—

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > Experts] (a) the claimant agrees;

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > Experts] (b) the court so directs; or

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > Experts] (c) the claimant’s expert report has been amended and the claimant is not prepared to disclose the original report.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > Experts] 7.9 Any party may send to an agreed expert written questions on the report, via the first party’s solicitors. Such questions must be put within 28 days of service of the expert’s report and must only be for the purpose of clarification of the report. The expert should send answers to the questions simultaneously to each party.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > Experts] 7.10 The cost of a report from an agreed expert will usually be paid by the instructing first party: the costs of the expert replying to questions will usually be borne by the party which asks the questions.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > Experts] 7.11 If necessary, after proceedings have commenced and with the permission of the court, the parties may obtain further expert reports. It would be for the court to decide whether the costs of more than one expert’s report should be recoverable.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > Experts] B. Claims for whiplash injury

## 7.12

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 7.12] 7.12.1 The provisions of this paragraph apply to any medical report in support of a claim for whiplash injury, whether or not it is part of a claim for other injuries.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 7.12] 7.12.2 Where there is also a claim for other injuries, the provisions of section A above apply to instructions to and reports from experts in respect of those other injuries. Section A above also applies in respect of the use of any non-medical experts.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 7.12] 7.12.3 In respect of a claim for a whiplash injury, the claimant must follow one of the procedures set out in paragraphs 7.12.4 to 7.12.6.

## 7.12.4

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 7.12.4] (a) The claimant must obtain a fixed cost medical report from an accredited medical expert who is instructed via a search of the online database of medical reporting organisations and medical experts held by MedCo (website at: www.medco.org.uk);

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 7.12.4] (b) in instructing an expert to provide a fixed cost medical report in a claim for whiplash injury, it is expected that in most cases the medical expert will not need to see any medical records;

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 7.12.4] (c) where the claimant lives outside England and Wales, but chooses to be examined for the purposes of a medical report in England and Wales, paragraphs (a) and (b) apply.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 7.12.4] 7.12.5 Where the claimant obtains a medical report in respect of a more serious injury suffered at the same time as the whiplash injury, the claimant may use that report instead of a report under paragraph 7.12.4 above provided that—

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 7.12.4] (a) the report is from a doctor who is listed on the General Medical Council’s Specialist Register; and

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 7.12.4] (b) the report provides evidence of the whiplash injury.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 7.12.4] 7.12.6 Unless paragraph 7.12.4(c) applies, where the claimant lives outside England and Wales, the medical report in respect of the claim for the whiplash injury (or, if there is more than one report, the first report) must be from a person who is recognised by the country in which they practise as—

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 7.12.4] (a) being a medical expert; and

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 7.12.4] (b) having the required qualifications for the purposes of diagnosis and prognosis of a whiplash injury.

## 7.12.7 The following definitions apply in paragraph 7.12 and in paragraphs 8.2 and 8.3—

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 7.12.7 The following definitions apply in paragraph 7.12 and in paragraphs 8.2 and 8.3—] (a) ‘associate’ means, in respect of a medical expert, a colleague, partner, director, employer or employee in the same practice and ‘associated with’ has the equivalent meaning;

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 7.12.7 The following definitions apply in paragraph 7.12 and in paragraphs 8.2 and 8.3—] (b) ‘accredited medical expert’ means a medical expert who is accredited by MedCo to provide medical reports in whiplash injury claims;

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 7.12.7 The following definitions apply in paragraph 7.12 and in paragraphs 8.2 and 8.3—] (c) ‘fixed cost medical report’ means a report in a whiplash injury claim which is from a medical expert who, save in exceptional circumstances—

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 7.12.7 The following definitions apply in paragraph 7.12 and in paragraphs 8.2 and 8.3—] (i) has not provided treatment to the claimant;

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 7.12.7 The following definitions apply in paragraph 7.12 and in paragraphs 8.2 and 8.3—] (ii) is not associated with any person who has provided treatment; and

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 7.12.7 The following definitions apply in paragraph 7.12 and in paragraphs 8.2 and 8.3—] (iii) does not propose or recommend treatment that they or an associate then provide;

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 7.12.7 The following definitions apply in paragraph 7.12 and in paragraphs 8.2 and 8.3—] (d) ‘MedCo’ means MedCo Registration Solutions; and

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 7.12.7 The following definitions apply in paragraph 7.12 and in paragraphs 8.2 and 8.3—] (e) ‘whiplash injury’ means an injury or injuries of soft tissue in the neck, back or shoulder suffered because of driver negligence as defined in section 1 of the Civil Liability Act 2018 and as further applied by section 3 of that Act to claims arising from a road traffic accident on or after 31 May 2021 and where the duration of the whiplash injury or any of the whiplash injuries—

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 7.12.7 The following definitions apply in paragraph 7.12 and in paragraphs 8.2 and 8.3—] (i) does not exceed, or is not likely to exceed, two years; or

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 7.12.7 The following definitions apply in paragraph 7.12 and in paragraphs 8.2 and 8.3—] (ii) would not have exceeded, or would not be likely to exceed, two years but for the claimant’s failure to take reasonable steps to mitigate its effect.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 7.12.7 The following definitions apply in paragraph 7.12 and in paragraphs 8.2 and 8.3—] To the top

## 8. Negotiations following an admission

## 8.1

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 8.1] 8.1.1  Where a defendant admits liability which has caused some damage, before proceedings are issued, the claimant should send to that defendant—

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 8.1] (a) any medical reports obtained under this Protocol on which the claimant relies; and

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 8.1] (b) a schedule of any past and future expenses and losses which are claimed, even if the schedule is necessarily provisional. The schedule should contain as much detail as reasonably practicable and should identify those losses that are ongoing. If the schedule is likely to be updated before the case is concluded, it should say so.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 8.1] 8.1.2  The claimant should delay issuing proceedings for 21 days from disclosure of (a) and (b) above (unless such delay would cause his claim to become time-barred), to enable the parties to consider whether the claim is capable of settlement.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 8.1] 8.2 CPR Part 36 permits claimants and defendants to make offers to settle pre-proceedings. Parties should always consider if it is appropriate to make a Part 36 Offer before issuing. If such an offer is made, the party making the offer must always try to supply sufficient evidence and/or information to enable the offer to be properly considered.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 8.1] The level of detail will depend on the value of the claim. Except for any claim for a whiplash injury (for which see paragraphs 7.12 above and 8.3 below), medical reports may not be necessary where there is no significant continuing injury and a detailed schedule may not be necessary in a low value case.

## 8.3

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 8.3] 8.3.1 In a claim that consists of or includes a claim for whiplash injury, the Whiplash Injury Regulations 2021 provide that—

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 8.3] (a) no offer may be made, invited or accepted by either party; and

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 8.3] (b) no payment may be made by the defendant or accepted by the claimant,

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 8.3] in respect of the claim for whiplash injury until after the fixed cost medical report has been disclosed.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 8.3] 8.3.2 Any claim for whiplash injury and, if relevant, minor psychological injuries suffered on the same occasion as the whiplash injury, will be valued by reference to the tariffs set out in the Whiplash Injury Regulations 2021.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 8.3] (“Whiplash injury” is defined in paragraph 7.12.7.)

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 8.3] To the top

## 9. Alternative Dispute Resolution

## 9.1

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 9.1] 9.1.1  Litigation should be a last resort. As part of this Protocol, the parties should consider whether negotiation or some other form of Alternative Dispute Resolution (“ADR”) might enable them to resolve their dispute without commencing proceedings.

## 9.1.2  Some of the options for resolving disputes without commencing proceedings are—

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 9.1.2  Some of the options for resolving disputes without commencing proceedings are—] (a) discussions and negotiation (which may or may not include making Part 36 Offers or providing an explanation and/or apology);

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 9.1.2  Some of the options for resolving disputes without commencing proceedings are—] (b) mediation, a third party facilitating a resolution;

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 9.1.2  Some of the options for resolving disputes without commencing proceedings are—] (c) arbitration, a third party deciding the dispute; and

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 9.1.2  Some of the options for resolving disputes without commencing proceedings are—] (d) early neutral evaluation, a third party giving an informed opinion on the dispute.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 9.1.2  Some of the options for resolving disputes without commencing proceedings are—] 9.1.3  If proceedings are issued, the parties may be required by the court to provide evidence that ADR has been considered. It is expressly recognised that no party can or should be forced to mediate or enter into any form of ADR but unreasonable refusal to consider ADR will be taken into account by the court when deciding who bears the costs of the proceedings.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 9.1.2  Some of the options for resolving disputes without commencing proceedings are—] 9.2 Information on mediation and other forms of ADR is available in the Jackson ADR Handbook (available from Oxford University Press) or at-

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 9.1.2  Some of the options for resolving disputes without commencing proceedings are—] https://www.gov.uk/guidance/a-guide-to-civil-mediation (opens in a new tab)

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 9.1.2  Some of the options for resolving disputes without commencing proceedings are—] To the top

## 10. Quantification of Loss – Special damages

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 10. Quantification of Loss – Special damages] 10.1 In all cases, if the defendant admits liability, the claimant will send to the defendant as soon as reasonably practicable a schedule of any past and future expenses and losses which he claims, even if the schedule is necessarily provisional. The schedule should contain as much detail as reasonably practicable and should identify those losses that are ongoing. If the schedule is likely to be updated before the case is concluded, it should say so. The claimant should keep the defendant informed as to the rate at which his financial loss is progressing throughout the entire Protocol period.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 10. Quantification of Loss – Special damages] To the top

## 11. Stocktake

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 11. Stocktake] 11.1 Where the procedure set out in this Protocol has not resolved the dispute between the parties, each party should undertake a review of its own positions and the strengths and weaknesses of its case. The parties should then together consider the evidence and the arguments in order to see whether litigation can be avoided or, if that is not possible, for the issues between the parties to be narrowed before proceedings are issued. Where the defendant is insured and the pre-action steps have been taken by the insurer, the insurer would normally be expected to nominate solicitors to act in the proceedings and to accept service of the claim form and other documents on behalf of the defendant. The claimant or their solicitor is recommended to invite the insurer to nominate the insurer to nominate solicitors to act in the proceedings and do so 7 to 14 days before the intended issue date.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > 11. Stocktake] To the top

## Annex C: Pre-Action Personal Injury Protocol Standard Disclosure Lists

## RTA CASES

## SECTION A

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > SECTION A] In all cases where liability is at issue–

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > SECTION A] (i) documents identifying nature, extent and location of damage to defendant’s vehicle where there is any dispute about point of impact;

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > SECTION A] (ii) MOT certificate where relevant;

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > SECTION A] (iii) maintenance records where vehicle defect is alleged or it is alleged by defendant that there was an unforeseen defect which caused or contributed to the accident.

## SECTION B

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > SECTION B] Accident involving commercial vehicle as defendant–

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > SECTION B] (i) tachograph charts or entry from individual control book;

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > SECTION B] (ii) maintenance and repair records required for operators’ licence where vehicle defect is alleged or it is alleged by defendant that there was an unforeseen defect which caused or contributed to the accident.

## SECTION C

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > SECTION C] Cases against local authorities where highway design defect is alleged—

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > SECTION C] (i) documents produced to comply with Section 39 of the Road Traffic Act 1988 in respect of the duty designed to promote road safety to include studies into road accidents in the relevant area and documents relating to measures recommended to prevent accidents in the relevant area;

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > SECTION C] (ii) any Rule 43 reports produced at the request of a coroner pursuant to Schedule 5 of the Coroners & Justice Act 2009, for accidents occurring in the same locus as one covered by an earlier report.

## HIGHWAY TRIPPING CLAIMS

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > HIGHWAY TRIPPING CLAIMS] Documents from Highway Authority for a period of 12 months prior to the accident–

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > HIGHWAY TRIPPING CLAIMS] (i) records of inspection for the relevant stretch of highway;

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > HIGHWAY TRIPPING CLAIMS] (ii) maintenance records including records of independent contractors working in relevant area;

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > HIGHWAY TRIPPING CLAIMS] (iii) records of the minutes of Highway Authority meetings where maintenance or repair policy has been discussed or decided;

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > HIGHWAY TRIPPING CLAIMS] (iv) records of complaints about the state of highways;

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > HIGHWAY TRIPPING CLAIMS] (v) records of other accidents which have occurred on the relevant stretch of highway.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > GENERAL DOCUMENTS] (i) accident book entry;

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > GENERAL DOCUMENTS] (ii) other entries in the book or other accident books, relating to accidents or injuries similar to those suffered by our client (and if it is contended there are no such entries please confirm we may have facilities to inspect all accident books);

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > GENERAL DOCUMENTS] (iii) first aider report;

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > GENERAL DOCUMENTS] (iv) surgery record;

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > GENERAL DOCUMENTS] (v) foreman/supervisor accident report;

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > GENERAL DOCUMENTS] (vi) safety representative’s accident report;

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > GENERAL DOCUMENTS] (vii) RIDDOR (Reporting of Injuries, Diseases and Dangerous Occurrences Regulations) reported to HSE or relevant investigatory agency;

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > GENERAL DOCUMENTS] (viii) back to work interview notes and report;

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > GENERAL DOCUMENTS] (ix) all personnel/occupational health records relating to our client;

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > GENERAL DOCUMENTS] (x) other communications between defendants and HSE or other relevant investigatory agency;

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > GENERAL DOCUMENTS] (xi) minutes of Health and Safety Committee meeting(s) where accident/matter considered;

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > GENERAL DOCUMENTS] (xii) copies of all relevant CCTV footage and any other relevant photographs, videos and/or DVDs;

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > GENERAL DOCUMENTS] (xiii) copies of all electronic communications/documentation relating to the accident;

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > GENERAL DOCUMENTS] (xiv) earnings information where defendant is employer;

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > GENERAL DOCUMENTS] (xv) reports to DWP;

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > GENERAL DOCUMENTS] (xvi) manufacturer’s or dealers instructions or recommendations concerning use of the work equipment;

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > GENERAL DOCUMENTS] (xvii) service or maintenance records of the work equipment;

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > GENERAL DOCUMENTS] (xviii) all documents recording arrangements for detecting, removing or cleaning up any articles or substances on the floor of the premises likely to cause a trip or slip;

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > GENERAL DOCUMENTS] (xix) work sheets and all other documents completed by or on behalf of those responsible for implementing the cleaning policy and recording work done;

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > GENERAL DOCUMENTS] (xx) all invoices, receipts and other documents relating to the purchase of relevant safety equipment to prevent a repetition of the accident;

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > GENERAL DOCUMENTS] (xxi) all correspondence, memoranda or other documentation received or brought into being concerning the condition or repair of the work equipment/the premises;

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > GENERAL DOCUMENTS] (xxii) all correspondence, instructions, estimates, invoices and other documentation submitted or received concerning repairs, remedial works or other works to the work equipment/the premises since the date of that accident;

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > GENERAL DOCUMENTS] (xxiii) work sheets and all other documents recording work done completed by those responsible for maintaining the work equipment/premises;

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > GENERAL DOCUMENTS] (xxiv) all relevant risk assessments;

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > GENERAL DOCUMENTS] (xxv) all reports, conclusions or recommendations following any enquiry or investigation into the accident;

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > GENERAL DOCUMENTS] (xxvi) the record kept of complaints made by employees together with all other documents recording in any way such complaints or actions taken thereon;

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > GENERAL DOCUMENTS] (xxvii) all other correspondence sent, or received, relating to our client’s injury prior to receipt of this letter of claim;

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > GENERAL DOCUMENTS] (xxviii) documents listed above relating to any previous/similar accident/matter identified by the claimant and relied upon as proof of negligence including accident book entries;

## ANNEX D: Letter of instruction to medical expert

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > ANNEX D: Letter of instruction to medical expert] Dear Sir,

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > ANNEX D: Letter of instruction to medical expert] Re: (Name and Address)

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > ANNEX D: Letter of instruction to medical expert] D.O.B.–

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > ANNEX D: Letter of instruction to medical expert] Telephone No.–

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > ANNEX D: Letter of instruction to medical expert] Date of Accident –

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > ANNEX D: Letter of instruction to medical expert] We are acting for the above named in connection with injuries received in an accident which occurred on the above date. A summary of the main facts of the accident circumstances is provided below. The main injuries appear to have been (describe main injuries and functional impact on day to day living as in Letter of Claim) .

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > ANNEX D: Letter of instruction to medical expert] In order to assist with the preparation of your report we have enclosed the following documents:

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > ANNEX D: Letter of instruction to medical expert] Enclosures

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > ANNEX D: Letter of instruction to medical expert] Hospital Records

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > ANNEX D: Letter of instruction to medical expert] GP records

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > ANNEX D: Letter of instruction to medical expert] Statement of Events

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > ANNEX D: Letter of instruction to medical expert] We have not obtained [ ] records yet but will use our best endeavours to obtain these without delay if you request them.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > ANNEX D: Letter of instruction to medical expert] We should be obliged if you would examine our Client and let us have a full and detailed report dealing with any relevant pre-accident medical history, the injuries sustained, treatment received and present condition, dealing in particular with the capacity for work and giving a prognosis.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > ANNEX D: Letter of instruction to medical expert] It is central to our assessment of the extent of our Client’s injuries to establish the extent and duration of any continuing disability. Accordingly, in the prognosis section we would ask you to specifically comment on any areas of continuing complaint or disability or impact on daily living. If there is such continuing disability you should comment upon the level of suffering or inconvenience caused and, if you are able, give your view as to when or if the complaint or disability is likely to resolve.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > ANNEX D: Letter of instruction to medical expert] If our client requires further treatment, please can you advise of the cost on a private patient basis.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > ANNEX D: Letter of instruction to medical expert] Please send our Client an appointment direct for this purpose. Should you be able to offer a cancellation appointment please contact our Client direct. We confirm we will be responsible for your reasonable fees.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > ANNEX D: Letter of instruction to medical expert] We are obtaining the notes and records from our Client’s GP and Hospitals attended and will forward them to you when they are to hand/or please request the GP and Hospital records direct and advise that any invoice for the provision of these records should be forwarded to us.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > ANNEX D: Letter of instruction to medical expert] In order to comply with Court Rules we would be grateful if you would insert above your signature, the following statement: “I confirm that I have made clear which facts and matters referred to in this report are within my own knowledge and which are not. Those that are within my own knowledge I confirm to be true. The opinions I have expressed represent my true and complete professional opinions on the matters to which they refer”.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > ANNEX D: Letter of instruction to medical expert] In order to avoid further correspondence we can confirm that on the evidence we have there is no reason to suspect we may be pursuing a claim against the hospital or its staff.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > ANNEX D: Letter of instruction to medical expert] We look forward to receiving your report within _______ weeks. If you will not be able to prepare your report within this period please telephone us upon receipt of these instructions.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > ANNEX D: Letter of instruction to medical expert] When acknowledging these instructions it would assist if you could give an estimate as to the likely time scale for the provision of your report and also an indication as to your fee.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > ANNEX D: Letter of instruction to medical expert] To the top

[Pre-Action Protocol for Personal Injury Claims > ANNEX D: Letter of instruction to medical expert] Yours faithfully,

# Pre-Action Protocol for Possession Claims based on Mortgage or Home Purchase Plan Arrears in Respect of Residential Property

[Pre-Action Protocol for Possession Claims based on Mortgage or Home Purchase Plan Arrears in Respect of Residential Property] Table of contents

## I INTRODUCTION

## Definitions

## 1.1 In this Protocol–

[Pre-Action Protocol for Possession Claims based on Mortgage or Home Purchase Plan Arrears in Respect of Residential Property > 1.1 In this Protocol–] (a) ‘possession claim’ means a claim for the recovery of possession of property under Part 55 of the Civil Procedure Rules 1998;

[Pre-Action Protocol for Possession Claims based on Mortgage or Home Purchase Plan Arrears in Respect of Residential Property > 1.1 In this Protocol–] (b) ‘home purchase plan’ means a method of purchasing a property by way of a sale and lease arrangement that does not require the payment of interest;

[Pre-Action Protocol for Possession Claims based on Mortgage or Home Purchase Plan Arrears in Respect of Residential Property > 1.1 In this Protocol–] (c) ‘bank holiday’ means a bank holiday under the Banking and Financial Dealings Act 1971;

[Pre-Action Protocol for Possession Claims based on Mortgage or Home Purchase Plan Arrears in Respect of Residential Property > 1.1 In this Protocol–] (d) ‘business day’ means any day except Saturday, Sunday, a bank holiday, Good Friday or Christmas day; and

[Pre-Action Protocol for Possession Claims based on Mortgage or Home Purchase Plan Arrears in Respect of Residential Property > 1.1 In this Protocol–] (e) ‘authorised tenant’ means a tenant whose tenancy is authorised as between the borrower and the lender.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Possession Claims based on Mortgage or Home Purchase Plan Arrears in Respect of Residential Property > 1.1 In this Protocol–] To the top

## Preamble

[Pre-Action Protocol for Possession Claims based on Mortgage or Home Purchase Plan Arrears in Respect of Residential Property > Preamble] 2.1 This Protocol describes the behaviour the court will normally expect of the parties prior to the start of a possession claim within the scope of paragraph 3.1 below.

## 2.2 This Protocol does not alter the parties’ rights and obligations.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Possession Claims based on Mortgage or Home Purchase Plan Arrears in Respect of Residential Property > 2.2 This Protocol does not alter the parties’ rights and obligations.] 2.3 It is in the interests of the parties that mortgage payments or payments under home purchase plans are made promptly and that difficulties are resolved wherever possible without court proceedings. However in some cases an order for possession may be in the interest of both the lender and the borrower.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Possession Claims based on Mortgage or Home Purchase Plan Arrears in Respect of Residential Property > 2.2 This Protocol does not alter the parties’ rights and obligations.] To the top

## Aims

## 3.1 The aims of this Protocol are to–

[Pre-Action Protocol for Possession Claims based on Mortgage or Home Purchase Plan Arrears in Respect of Residential Property > 3.1 The aims of this Protocol are to–] (a) ensure that a lender or home purchase plan provider (in this Protocol collectively referred to as ‘the lender’) and a borrower or home purchase plan customer (in this Protocol collectively referred to as ‘the borrower’) act fairly and reasonably with each other in resolving any matter concerning mortgage or home purchase plan arrears;

[Pre-Action Protocol for Possession Claims based on Mortgage or Home Purchase Plan Arrears in Respect of Residential Property > 3.1 The aims of this Protocol are to–] (b) encourage greater pre-action contact between the lender and the borrower in order to seek agreement between the parties, and where agreement cannot be reached, to enable efficient use of the court’s time and resources; and

[Pre-Action Protocol for Possession Claims based on Mortgage or Home Purchase Plan Arrears in Respect of Residential Property > 3.1 The aims of this Protocol are to–] (c) encourage lenders to check who is in occupation of the property before issuing proceedings.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Possession Claims based on Mortgage or Home Purchase Plan Arrears in Respect of Residential Property > 3.1 The aims of this Protocol are to–] 3.2 Where either party is required to communicate and provide information to the other, reasonable steps should be taken to do so in a way that is clear, fair and not misleading. If the lender is aware that the borrower may have difficulties in reading or understanding the information provided, the lender should take reasonable steps to ensure that information is communicated in a way that the borrower can understand.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Possession Claims based on Mortgage or Home Purchase Plan Arrears in Respect of Residential Property > 3.1 The aims of this Protocol are to–] To the top

## Scope

## 4.1 This Protocol applies to arrears on–

[Pre-Action Protocol for Possession Claims based on Mortgage or Home Purchase Plan Arrears in Respect of Residential Property > 4.1 This Protocol applies to arrears on–] (a) first charge residential mortgages and home purchase plans regulated by the Financial Conduct Authority under the Financial Services and Markets Act 2000 (as amended by the Financial Services Act, 2012);

[Pre-Action Protocol for Possession Claims based on Mortgage or Home Purchase Plan Arrears in Respect of Residential Property > 4.1 This Protocol applies to arrears on–] (b) second charge mortgages over residential property and other secured loans regulated under the Consumer Credit Act 1974 on residential property; and

[Pre-Action Protocol for Possession Claims based on Mortgage or Home Purchase Plan Arrears in Respect of Residential Property > 4.1 This Protocol applies to arrears on–] (c) unregulated residential mortgages.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Possession Claims based on Mortgage or Home Purchase Plan Arrears in Respect of Residential Property > 4.1 This Protocol applies to arrears on–] 4.2 Where a potential claim includes a money claim and a possession claim, this protocol applies to both.

## 4.3 The protocol does not apply to Buy To Let mortgages.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Possession Claims based on Mortgage or Home Purchase Plan Arrears in Respect of Residential Property > 4.3 The protocol does not apply to Buy To Let mortgages.] To the top

## II ACTIONS PRIOR TO THE START OF A POSSESSION CLAIM

## Initial contact and provision of information

## 5.1 Where a borrower falls into arrears, the lender must provide the borrower with—

[Pre-Action Protocol for Possession Claims based on Mortgage or Home Purchase Plan Arrears in Respect of Residential Property > 5.1 Where a borrower falls into arrears, the lender must provide the borrower with—] (a) where appropriate, the required regulatory information sheet or the National Homelessness Advice Service/Shelter/Cymru booklet on mortgage arrears;

[Pre-Action Protocol for Possession Claims based on Mortgage or Home Purchase Plan Arrears in Respect of Residential Property > 5.1 Where a borrower falls into arrears, the lender must provide the borrower with—] (b) information on the current monthly instalments and the amounts paid for the last 2 years; and

[Pre-Action Protocol for Possession Claims based on Mortgage or Home Purchase Plan Arrears in Respect of Residential Property > 5.1 Where a borrower falls into arrears, the lender must provide the borrower with—] (c) information on the amount of arrears, which should include–

[Pre-Action Protocol for Possession Claims based on Mortgage or Home Purchase Plan Arrears in Respect of Residential Property > 5.1 Where a borrower falls into arrears, the lender must provide the borrower with—] (i) the total amount of the arrears;

[Pre-Action Protocol for Possession Claims based on Mortgage or Home Purchase Plan Arrears in Respect of Residential Property > 5.1 Where a borrower falls into arrears, the lender must provide the borrower with—] (ii) the total outstanding of the mortgage or the home purchase plan; and

[Pre-Action Protocol for Possession Claims based on Mortgage or Home Purchase Plan Arrears in Respect of Residential Property > 5.1 Where a borrower falls into arrears, the lender must provide the borrower with—] (iii) whether interest or charges have been or will be added, and, where appropriate, details or an estimate of the interest or charges that may be payable.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Possession Claims based on Mortgage or Home Purchase Plan Arrears in Respect of Residential Property > 5.1 Where a borrower falls into arrears, the lender must provide the borrower with—] 5.2 The lender should also seek information about whether the property is occupied by an authorised tenant.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Possession Claims based on Mortgage or Home Purchase Plan Arrears in Respect of Residential Property > 5.1 Where a borrower falls into arrears, the lender must provide the borrower with—] 5.3 The lender must advise the borrower to make early contact with the housing department of the borrower’s Local Authority and, should, where relevant refer the borrower to appropriate sources of independent debt advice.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Possession Claims based on Mortgage or Home Purchase Plan Arrears in Respect of Residential Property > 5.1 Where a borrower falls into arrears, the lender must provide the borrower with—] 5.4 The parties, or their representatives, must take all reasonable steps to discuss with each other the reasons for the arrears, the borrower’s financial circumstances and proposals for repayment of the arrears (see paragraph 7.1). For example, parties should consider whether the reasons for the arrears are temporary or long-term, and whether the borrower may be able to pay the arrears in a reasonable time.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Possession Claims based on Mortgage or Home Purchase Plan Arrears in Respect of Residential Property > 5.1 Where a borrower falls into arrears, the lender must provide the borrower with—] 5.5 The lender must consider a reasonable request from the borrower to change the date of regular payment (within the same payment period) or the method by which payment is made. The lender must either agree to such a request or, where it refuses such a request, it must, within a reasonable period of time, give the borrower a written explanation of its reasons for the refusal.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Possession Claims based on Mortgage or Home Purchase Plan Arrears in Respect of Residential Property > 5.1 Where a borrower falls into arrears, the lender must provide the borrower with—] 5.6 The lender must respond promptly to any proposal for payment made by the borrower. If the lender does not agree to such a proposal it should give reasons in writing to the borrower within 10 business days of the proposal.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Possession Claims based on Mortgage or Home Purchase Plan Arrears in Respect of Residential Property > 5.1 Where a borrower falls into arrears, the lender must provide the borrower with—] 5.7 If the lender submits a proposal for payment, the borrower must be given a reasonable period of time in which to consider such proposals. The lender must set out the proposal in sufficient detail to enable the borrower to understand the implications of the proposal.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Possession Claims based on Mortgage or Home Purchase Plan Arrears in Respect of Residential Property > 5.1 Where a borrower falls into arrears, the lender must provide the borrower with—] 5.8 If the borrower fails to comply with an agreement, the lender should warn the borrower, by giving the borrower 15 business days notice in writing, of its intention to start a possession claim unless the borrower remedies the breach in the agreement.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Possession Claims based on Mortgage or Home Purchase Plan Arrears in Respect of Residential Property > 5.1 Where a borrower falls into arrears, the lender must provide the borrower with—] To the top

## Postponing the start of a possession claim

[Pre-Action Protocol for Possession Claims based on Mortgage or Home Purchase Plan Arrears in Respect of Residential Property > Postponing the start of a possession claim] 6.1 A lender must not consider starting a possession claim for mortgage arrears where the borrower can demonstrate to the lender that the borrower has–

[Pre-Action Protocol for Possession Claims based on Mortgage or Home Purchase Plan Arrears in Respect of Residential Property > Postponing the start of a possession claim] (a) submitted a claim to–

[Pre-Action Protocol for Possession Claims based on Mortgage or Home Purchase Plan Arrears in Respect of Residential Property > Postponing the start of a possession claim] (i) the Department for Works and Pensions (‘DWP’) for Support for Mortgage Interest (SMI) or if appropriate Universal Credit; or

[Pre-Action Protocol for Possession Claims based on Mortgage or Home Purchase Plan Arrears in Respect of Residential Property > Postponing the start of a possession claim] (ii) an insurer under a mortgage payment protection policy; or

[Pre-Action Protocol for Possession Claims based on Mortgage or Home Purchase Plan Arrears in Respect of Residential Property > Postponing the start of a possession claim] (iii) a participating local authority for support under a Mortgage Rescue Scheme, or other means of homelessness prevention support provided by the local authority,

[Pre-Action Protocol for Possession Claims based on Mortgage or Home Purchase Plan Arrears in Respect of Residential Property > Postponing the start of a possession claim] (iv) and has provided all the evidence required to process a claim;

[Pre-Action Protocol for Possession Claims based on Mortgage or Home Purchase Plan Arrears in Respect of Residential Property > Postponing the start of a possession claim] (b) a reasonable expectation of eligibility for payment from the DWP or from an insurer or support from the local authority or welfare or charitable organisation such as the Veterans Welfare Scheme or Royal British Legion;

[Pre-Action Protocol for Possession Claims based on Mortgage or Home Purchase Plan Arrears in Respect of Residential Property > Postponing the start of a possession claim] (c) an ability to pay a mortgage instalment not covered by a claim to the DWP or the insurer in relation to a claim under paragraph 6.1(1)(a) or (b);

[Pre-Action Protocol for Possession Claims based on Mortgage or Home Purchase Plan Arrears in Respect of Residential Property > Postponing the start of a possession claim] (d) difficulty in respect of affordability or another specific personal or financial difficulty, and requires time to seek free independent debt advice, or has a confirmed appointment with a debt adviser and

[Pre-Action Protocol for Possession Claims based on Mortgage or Home Purchase Plan Arrears in Respect of Residential Property > Postponing the start of a possession claim] (e) a reasonable expectation, providing evidence where possible, of an improvement in their financial circumstances in the foreseeable future ( for example a new job or increased income from a lodger).

[Pre-Action Protocol for Possession Claims based on Mortgage or Home Purchase Plan Arrears in Respect of Residential Property > Postponing the start of a possession claim] 6.2 If a borrower can demonstrate that reasonable steps have been or will be taken to market the property at an appropriate price in accordance with reasonable professional advice, the lender must consider postponing starting a possession claim to allow the borrower a realistic period of time to sell the property. The borrower must continue to take all reasonable steps actively to market the property where the lender has agreed to postpone starting a possession claim.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Possession Claims based on Mortgage or Home Purchase Plan Arrears in Respect of Residential Property > Postponing the start of a possession claim] 6.3 Where, notwithstanding paragraphs 6.1 an 6.2, the lender has agreed to postpone starting a possession claim, the borrower should provide the lender with a copy of the particulars of sale, the Energy Performance Certificate (‘EPC’) or proof that an EPC has been commissioned and (where relevant) details of purchase offers received within a reasonable period of time specified by the lender. The borrower should give the lender details of the estate agent and the conveyancer instructed to deal with the sale. The borrower should also authorise the estate agent and the conveyancer to communicate with the lender about the progress of the sale and the borrower’s conduct during the process.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Possession Claims based on Mortgage or Home Purchase Plan Arrears in Respect of Residential Property > Postponing the start of a possession claim] 6.4 Where the lender decides not to postpone the start of a possession claim, it must inform the borrower of the reasons for this decision at least 5 business days before starting proceedings.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Possession Claims based on Mortgage or Home Purchase Plan Arrears in Respect of Residential Property > Postponing the start of a possession claim] To the top

## Further matters to consider before starting a possession claim

[Pre-Action Protocol for Possession Claims based on Mortgage or Home Purchase Plan Arrears in Respect of Residential Property > Further matters to consider before starting a possession claim] 7.1 Starting a possession claim should be a last resort and must not normally be started unless all other reasonable attempts to resolve the situation have failed. The parties should consider whether, given the individual circumstances of the borrower and the form of the agreement, it is reasonable and appropriate to do one or more of the following–

[Pre-Action Protocol for Possession Claims based on Mortgage or Home Purchase Plan Arrears in Respect of Residential Property > Further matters to consider before starting a possession claim] (a) extend the term of the mortgage;

[Pre-Action Protocol for Possession Claims based on Mortgage or Home Purchase Plan Arrears in Respect of Residential Property > Further matters to consider before starting a possession claim] (b) change the type of mortgage;

[Pre-Action Protocol for Possession Claims based on Mortgage or Home Purchase Plan Arrears in Respect of Residential Property > Further matters to consider before starting a possession claim] (c) defer payment of interest due under the mortgage;

[Pre-Action Protocol for Possession Claims based on Mortgage or Home Purchase Plan Arrears in Respect of Residential Property > Further matters to consider before starting a possession claim] (d) capitalise the arrears; or

[Pre-Action Protocol for Possession Claims based on Mortgage or Home Purchase Plan Arrears in Respect of Residential Property > Further matters to consider before starting a possession claim] (e) make use of any Government forbearance initiatives in which the lender chooses to participate.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Possession Claims based on Mortgage or Home Purchase Plan Arrears in Respect of Residential Property > Further matters to consider before starting a possession claim] 7.2 Where there is an authorised tenant in occupation of the property, at the possession hearing the court will consider whether—

[Pre-Action Protocol for Possession Claims based on Mortgage or Home Purchase Plan Arrears in Respect of Residential Property > Further matters to consider before starting a possession claim] (a) further directions are required;

[Pre-Action Protocol for Possession Claims based on Mortgage or Home Purchase Plan Arrears in Respect of Residential Property > Further matters to consider before starting a possession claim] (b) to adjourn the possession claim until possession has been recovered against the tenant; or

[Pre-Action Protocol for Possession Claims based on Mortgage or Home Purchase Plan Arrears in Respect of Residential Property > Further matters to consider before starting a possession claim] (c) to make an order conditional upon the tenant’s right of occupation.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Possession Claims based on Mortgage or Home Purchase Plan Arrears in Respect of Residential Property > Further matters to consider before starting a possession claim] To the top

## Complaints to the Financial Services Ombudsman

[Pre-Action Protocol for Possession Claims based on Mortgage or Home Purchase Plan Arrears in Respect of Residential Property > Complaints to the Financial Services Ombudsman] 8.1 The lender must consider whether to postpone the start of a possession claim where the borrower has made a genuine complaint to the Financial Ombudsman Service (‘FOS’) about the potential possession claim.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Possession Claims based on Mortgage or Home Purchase Plan Arrears in Respect of Residential Property > Complaints to the Financial Services Ombudsman] 8.2 Where a lender does not intend to await the decision of the FOS, it must give notice to the borrower, with reasons, that it intends to start a possession claim.

[Pre-Action Protocol for Possession Claims based on Mortgage or Home Purchase Plan Arrears in Respect of Residential Property > Complaints to the Financial Services Ombudsman] To the top

[Pre-Action Protocol for Possession Claims based on Mortgage or Home Purchase Plan Arrears in Respect of Residential Property > Complaints to the Financial Services Ombudsman] Updated: Monday, 30 January 2017
